modules.title: Module 1: The Marriage of Anansewa (Efua T. Sutherland) - Africa
modules.html:
1.1 Background and Form

Efua Theodora Sutherland (1924–1996) was a Ghanaian dramatist, teacher and founder of the Ghana Drama Studio. The Marriage of Anansewa (published 1975) is subtitled a storytelling drama. Sutherland created the form she named Anansegoro, a stage development of the Akan oral Anansesem (Ananse stories) told at moonlight gatherings.

Features of Anansegoro to remember:

  • A Storyteller who narrates, comments, teases the audience and moves the plot along.
  • Mboguo – songs, drumming and dance interludes performed by the players and audience, which comment on the action and mark transitions.
  • Deliberate audience participation; the fourth wall is broken from the first line.
  • The trickster hero Ananse, spider-man, symbol of human ingenuity, greed and survival wit.
  • Blend of Akan proverbs, praise names, libation and modern items (telephone, typewriter, taxi) that place the play in a changing post-independence Ghana.

1.2 Plot Summary by Act

ActAction
Act IAnanse, poor but resourceful, dictates letters to his daughter Anansewa, offering her hand in marriage to four wealthy chiefs at once: Chief-Who-Is-Chief, Togbe Klu IV, Sapaase Chief and Mines Chief. He hopes for a flood of gifts. Anansewa, typing the letters, is uneasy. Ananse justifies himself in a long address to the audience about his poverty and his ambitions for his daughter's education.
Act IIGifts and messengers pour in from the four chiefs. Ananse's house is transformed: money, cloth, drink, building materials. Aya (Ananse's mother) and Ekuwa (his aunt) arrive; the outdooring/puberty rite for Anansewa is performed with singing and dance. Christie, an attractive and shrewd woman, appears, courting Ananse. The comedy of accumulation reaches its height, but so does the danger: all four chiefs now expect the same bride.
Act IIIThe trap closes. Messengers announce that the chiefs are coming to claim Anansewa. Ananse must extricate himself. He devises the deception: Anansewa is to feign death. Property and prestige must be preserved without a wedding to the wrong man. Ananse prepares the household, rehearsing grief with theatrical care.
Act IVThe 'death' is announced. Three chiefs respond with cold formality or with insult, sending mere token messages, while Chief-Who-Is-Chief's messenger arrives with genuine sorrow, full mourning gifts and love. Ananse thus proves which suitor is worthy. Anansewa 'revives' — the miracle is credited to the sincerity of true love — and is betrothed to Chief-Who-Is-Chief. The play ends in song, dance and general rejoicing.

1.3 Characterisation

  • Ananse – protagonist and trickster: intelligent, eloquent, manipulative, greedy yet loving, a survivor of poverty. He is both admired and criticised; the play lets the audience laugh at him while recognising him as 'Everyman' in a hard economy.
  • Anansewa – obedient daughter, educated (secretarial training), intelligent and increasingly assertive; she questions her father's scheme and consents only in love.
  • Christie – worldly, calculating, self-assured; she becomes Ananse's ally and match, and stage-manages part of the deception.
  • Aya – Ananse's mother, custodian of tradition, blunt and morally alert.
  • Ekuwa – Ananse's aunt, comic, traditional, concerned with propriety.
  • The Storyteller – narrator, chorus and interpreter; controls pace and audience response.
  • The four chiefs – mostly represented by messengers, they embody different degrees of wealth, pomposity and sincerity; only Chief-Who-Is-Chief shows genuine feeling.

1.4 Themes

  1. Materialism and the commercialisation of marriage – bride-wealth is turned into a business venture.
  2. Poverty and survival by wit – Ananse's schemes grow out of economic desperation.
  3. Parental responsibility and the education of the girl-child.
  4. Tradition in transition – libation and puberty rites coexist with telephones and typewriters.
  5. Love and sincerity as the true test of worth.
  6. Deception, its uses and its dangers.
  7. Community and communal art – the audience is part of the performance.

1.5 Style and Dramatic Technique

Episodic storytelling structure; direct address; mboguo songs; proverbs and Akan idiom in English; comic exaggeration; suspense created by the multiplying suitors; symbolic use of the spider's web (the plot Ananse weaves and is nearly caught in); poetic libation language; and a festive, participatory ending typical of comedy.

examples.q: Discuss the dramatic significance of the mboguo in The Marriage of Anansewa.
examples.a: The mboguo are the interpolated songs, drumming and dance that punctuate the play. Dramatically they perform at least five functions. First, they mark transitions between episodes, taking over the work done by scene changes in Western realistic drama. Second, they comment on the action like a Greek chorus, either praising, warning or mocking Ananse, so that the audience is guided towards a moral judgement without an explicit sermon. Third, they secure audience participation: because the songs are drawn from familiar Akan performance culture, spectators join in and become co-performers, which is the essence of Anansegoro. Fourth, they regulate mood, relieving tension after the anxieties of Act III and expanding the joy of the final betrothal. Fifth, they root the play in Ghanaian tradition, asserting that African drama need not imitate the European stage to be serious art.

examples.q: How does Sutherland use the feigned death of Anansewa to resolve the plot?
examples.a: The feigned death is Ananse's masterstroke and the play's structural climax. Having promised one daughter to four chiefs, Ananse faces exposure and possible ruin; a 'dead' bride cannot be claimed, so the deception buys him escape. More importantly, it becomes a moral test. The reactions of the suitors to the news function as an examination of character: three send perfunctory or grudging messages that reveal their interest was in possession and prestige, while Chief-Who-Is-Chief responds with unfeigned grief and full mourning gifts, proving genuine affection. Anansewa's 'resurrection' then reads symbolically: love restores life, and the marriage that follows is presented as deserved rather than purchased. The device thus converts a comic escape into a statement about the difference between buying a wife and loving a woman.

modules.title: Module 2: An Inspector Calls (J. B. Priestley) - Non-Africa
modules.html:
2.1 Background

John Boynton Priestley (1894–1984) wrote An Inspector Calls in 1945, at the end of the Second World War, but set it in 1912, in the fictional industrial city of Brumley in the North Midlands of England. The gap between the setting and the writing is deliberate: the 1912 audience on stage is confident and complacent, while the 1945 audience in the theatre knows that two world wars, the sinking of the Titanic and the Great Depression lie ahead. Priestley was a socialist who believed in collective responsibility and the welfare state.

2.2 Plot: Act-by-Act

ActAction and Function
Act OneThe Birlings celebrate Sheila's engagement to Gerald Croft. Arthur Birling lectures the young men on individualism ('a man has to make his own way') and dismisses talk of war and of the 'unsinkable' Titanic. Inspector Goole arrives: a girl, Eva Smith, has died in the infirmary after swallowing disinfectant. Birling admits sacking her in 1910 for leading a demand for higher wages. Sheila then admits she had Eva dismissed from Milwards out of jealousy and spite. The name 'Daisy Renton' makes Gerald react.
Act TwoGerald confesses his affair with Daisy Renton, whom he kept as his mistress and abandoned; Sheila returns the ring. Mrs Sybil Birling, chair of a women's charity, is exposed as having refused help to the pregnant girl and having insisted the father be made responsible. Unaware, she denounces the young father as a drunken idler who should be made an example of — damning her own son.
Act ThreeEric admits he forced his way into the girl's lodgings, made her pregnant and stole money from the family firm to support her. The Inspector delivers his final speech: 'We are members of one body... if men will not learn that lesson, then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish.' He leaves. The family discovers no Inspector Goole is on the force and no girl died that night; Birling, Mrs Birling and Gerald celebrate their escape while Sheila and Eric insist the guilt remains. The telephone rings: a girl has just died and a police inspector is on his way. Curtain.

2.3 Characterisation

  • Arthur Birling – wealthy factory owner, socially ambitious, unteachable; a mouthpiece for capitalist individualism, undermined by dramatic irony.
  • Sybil Birling – cold, class-proud, socially superior to her husband; her charity is charity without compassion.
  • Sheila Birling – initially spoilt but morally sensitive; she accepts responsibility fully and becomes the Inspector's echo in Act Three.
  • Eric Birling – alcoholic, immature, guilty of assault and theft, yet capable of shame and change.
  • Gerald Croft – charming aristocratic fiancé; genuinely kind to Daisy for a time but ultimately closes ranks with the older generation.
  • Inspector Goole – mysterious, morally authoritative, controls the pace of revelation ('One person and one line of inquiry at a time'). The pun 'Goole/ghoul' suggests he is a supernatural or symbolic figure — conscience, judgement, or the voice of the future.
  • Eva Smith / Daisy Renton – never appears; her generic name makes her a representative of 'millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths'.

2.4 Themes

  1. Social responsibility versus individualism – the play's central argument.
  2. Class and exploitation – the poor are used economically and sexually.
  3. Gender and the position of women – Eva has neither economic nor legal protection.
  4. Generational conflict – the young can change; the old cannot.
  5. Guilt, conscience and confession.
  6. Appearance versus reality – respectability conceals cruelty.
  7. Time, consequence and moral judgement – the cyclical ending.

2.5 Dramatic Technique

Priestley observes the three unities (one place — the dining room; one continuous time; one action — the inquiry). He uses a well-made-play structure with each act ending on a cliff-hanger, sustained dramatic irony (Birling on the Titanic and on there being no war), a morality-play pattern of confession, the photograph shown to one character at a time to control testimony, and lighting that is 'pink and intimate' before the Inspector arrives and 'brighter and harder' afterwards. The cyclical ending turns the whole play into an unanswered summons.

examples.q: Examine the use of dramatic irony in Act One of An Inspector Calls.
examples.a: Priestley loads Birling's opening speeches with statements that the 1945 audience knows to be false. He declares the Titanic 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable' — the ship sank weeks after the play's April 1912 setting. He dismisses 'these silly little war scares' and predicts peace and prosperity by 1940, when in fact two world wars intervened. He assures Gerald and Eric that 'a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own', the very creed the Inspector will demolish. The irony has three effects: it destroys Birling's credibility before the moral argument even begins, so the audience distrusts everything he later says in self-defence; it establishes Priestley's thesis that confident capitalist individualism is blind to the future; and it creates a superior alliance between playwright and audience, who watch the family from the vantage point of history. The irony is thus not decorative but structural — the plot's moral verdict is delivered in advance.

examples.q: Comment on the significance of the final telephone call.
examples.a: The telephone call reverses the family's relief and restarts the whole action. Structurally it is a coup de theatre: the Birlings have just persuaded themselves that Goole was a hoax and that no lesson need be learnt, and the ringing telephone announces that a girl has died on her way to the infirmary and a real inspector is coming to ask questions. Thematically it enacts the Inspector's warning that those who refuse the lesson 'will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish'. It also supports Priestley's interest in time theories: the evening may be a rehearsal, a warning replayed until it is heeded. Morally it separates the characters permanently — Sheila and Eric, who accepted guilt without proof, are vindicated, while Birling, Mrs Birling and Gerald, whose repentance depended on the fear of scandal, are exposed. Finally, it transfers the summons to the audience, who leave the theatre knowing the inquiry is not over.

modules.title: Module 3: Comparative Study and Essay Practice
modules.html:
3.1 Comparing the Two Plays

AspectThe Marriage of AnansewaAn Inspector Calls
TypeComedy / storytelling drama (Anansegoro)Social-problem play with elements of mystery and morality drama
SettingPost-independence Ghana, Ananse's house and chiefly domainsBrumley, England, April 1912, one dining room
StructureFour episodic acts with songs and narrationThree tight acts observing the unities, each ending in a cliff-hanger
Narrative deviceStoryteller and mboguoInspector as questioner; photograph as controlling prop
Central figureAnanse, trickster survivorInspector Goole, moral judge
Social targetMaterialism, commercialised marriageClass exploitation and social irresponsibility
EndingFestive betrothal, reconciliationCyclical, unresolved, disturbing
Audience relationDirect participationIronic superiority, then implication

3.2 Shared Concerns

  • Both examine the treatment of a young woman by powerful men — Anansewa is auctioned, Eva Smith is used and discarded.
  • Both expose money as a distorting force in human relations.
  • Both use a controlling figure (Ananse / the Inspector) who arranges revelations for the audience.
  • Both end with a test that separates sincerity from pretence.
  • They differ in tone: Sutherland corrects through laughter, Priestley through indictment.

3.3 Essay Skeleton (Character Question)

  1. Introduction: place the character in the play and state your line of argument.
  2. Point 1: role in the plot, with an incident.
  3. Point 2: dominant traits, with a short quotation.
  4. Point 3: relationships with other characters.
  5. Point 4: thematic significance — what idea the character embodies.
  6. Conclusion: evaluative judgement answering the exact wording of the question.

examples.q: Compare the presentation of the powerless young woman in The Marriage of Anansewa and An Inspector Calls.
examples.a: Both plays place a young woman at the centre of a transaction conducted by others. Anansewa is educated and present on stage, but her marriage is negotiated behind her back and she is effectively offered for sale to four chiefs; her body and her future become her father's economic assets. Eva Smith is absent altogether — she has no lines, no appearance, and even her name changes to Daisy Renton — and this absence is itself a comment: the working-class woman is spoken about, never heard. The difference lies in agency and outcome. Anansewa gradually asserts herself, refuses to be a commodity, and the comic form grants her a marriage of affection; the ending affirms that love must validate custom. Eva has no such recourse: dismissed by an employer, sacked at a shop, used by a lover, made pregnant by another and refused charity by a committee, she dies. Sutherland's comedy allows reform within the family; Priestley's problem play insists that the entire social system, not one father, is on trial.

quiz.q: The Marriage of Anansewa was written by
quiz.solution: Efua Theodora Sutherland, the Ghanaian dramatist and founder of the Ghana Drama Studio, wrote the play, published in 1975.

quiz.q: Sutherland's term for her stage form based on Akan storytelling is
quiz.solution: Anansegoro is the dramatised stage form Sutherland developed from the oral Anansesem tradition; mboguo are the songs within it.

quiz.q: How many chiefs does Ananse offer his daughter to in marriage?
quiz.solution: Ananse writes to four chiefs: Chief-Who-Is-Chief, Togbe Klu IV, the Sapaase Chief and the Mines Chief.

quiz.q: The songs and dance interludes that punctuate The Marriage of Anansewa are called
quiz.solution: Mboguo are the interpolated songs, drumming and dance which comment on the action and secure audience participation.

quiz.q: Which suitor eventually wins Anansewa's hand?
quiz.solution: Chief-Who-Is-Chief alone responds to news of Anansewa's 'death' with genuine grief and full mourning gifts, proving sincere love.

quiz.q: Ananse's plan to escape the four suitors is to
options: make Anansewa pretend to be dead
quiz.solution: The feigned death both prevents any chief from claiming the bride and tests the sincerity of all four.

quiz.q: Christie's chief function in the play is to
options: serve as Ananse's shrewd ally and romantic match
quiz.solution: Christie is worldly and calculating; she courts Ananse and assists in stage-managing the deception, matching him in cunning.

quiz.q: An Inspector Calls is set in the year
quiz.solution: The play is set in spring 1912 although Priestley wrote it in 1945, a gap that generates the play's dramatic irony.

quiz.q: Mr Birling's confident claim that the Titanic is 'absolutely unsinkable' is an example of
quiz.solution: The audience knows the Titanic sank, so Birling's confidence exposes him; the gap between his knowledge and the audience's is dramatic irony.

quiz.q: Eva Smith is dismissed from Birling's works because she
options: led a demand for higher wages
quiz.solution: Birling sacked her as a ringleader of the strike for a small wage increase, which begins the chain of events.

quiz.q: Sheila causes Eva's dismissal from Milwards out of
options: jealousy and spite over a dress
quiz.solution: Sheila, annoyed that the dress suited Eva better than herself, abused her position as a valued customer to have her sacked.

quiz.q: Mrs Birling's role at the women's charity is significant because she
options: refused Eva help and blamed the child's father
quiz.solution: As chair of the committee she used her influence to reject Eva's appeal and demanded the father be made responsible, unaware it was Eric.

quiz.q: Eric's crimes against Eva Smith include
options: theft from the family firm and forcing himself upon her
quiz.solution: Eric admits he forced his way into her lodgings while drunk, made her pregnant, and stole money from Birling and Company to support her.

quiz.q: The name 'Goole' is significant because it suggests
quiz.solution: The homophone 'ghoul' hints that the Inspector is not an ordinary policeman but a symbolic or supernatural embodiment of conscience and judgement.

quiz.q: The lighting at the start of An Inspector Calls should be
options: pink and intimate, then brighter and harder
quiz.solution: Priestley's stage direction requires pink, intimate lighting for the celebration, changing to brighter and harder light when the Inspector arrives, symbolising interrogation and exposure.

quiz.q: The final telephone call reveals that
options: the Inspector was a real policeman
a girl has just died and an inspector is coming
quiz.solution: The cyclical ending announces a real death and a real inspector, reactivating the moral summons the family had dismissed.

quiz.q: Which pair of characters accepts responsibility permanently?
quiz.solution: Only the younger Birlings, Sheila and Eric, retain their sense of guilt after learning the Inspector may have been a hoax.

quiz.q: The central theme of An Inspector Calls is best stated as
options: collective social responsibility against selfish individualism
quiz.solution: The Inspector's closing speech, 'We are members of one body', crystallises Priestley's argument for social responsibility over Birling's individualism.

quiz.q: An Inspector Calls observes the three unities of
quiz.solution: The play keeps one continuous action (the inquiry), one continuous evening, and one location (the Birling dining room).

quiz.q: The eventual moral test of the suitors in The Marriage of Anansewa reveals that
options: wealth is the true measure of a husband
only sincere love deserves the bride
quiz.solution: Only Chief-Who-Is-Chief mourns sincerely, and the play awards the marriage to genuine affection rather than to the richest bidder.
